title: The Louisiana Weekly warning about audience behavior at the Lyons Fieldhouse show
summary: Tex interprets an April 1956 Weekly column scolding fans for dancing in the aisles at a Fats Domino, Ruth Brown and Little Richard concert.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I want you to read something. This is something from the Weekly. I think we talked about this.
Something that came out of Louisiana Weekly.
And we talked about this before.
Or talking about slightly disturbed at reports which reached the unsatisfied instead of letting their head down and getting just downright colored, C-U-L-U-D. I don't know who wrote that.
No, well, that's how it was in the Weekly.
That's how it was spelled. I was careful.

Well, they're talking about that type of public conduct only helps the arguments which the other side presents against the thing which is fighting so hard to secure. Let's stop dancing in the aisles, jumping up in the seats. Well, I think...
What's the... It seems that the paper's kind of talking down.

Well, you see, you're dealing with people like Rip Roberts who promoted, I think, the incident at the Lowler Fieldhouse with Fats Domino, Ruth Brown, Little Richard, Little Willie, John, the Clovers, John, Little Willie, John, the Clovers, the Turbans, Al Jackson, Joe Medlin, the Cadillacs, and Choker Campbell. Now, what they had reference to, now, if memory serves me correctly, since this came out the Louisiana Weekly, this was written by one of the social writers, I don't know what one, at that time, in that date. Because the show was going on, and I guess we were trying to elevate ourselves to a higher level of social acceptance rather than sit there and go through a lot of wild gyrations. Well, most of the people in the audience was very cool that night for some particular reason. They didn't get all excited like the rap people and like they do on television today because, you see, either, look, things have changed so much, even the clothing style has changed, even walking through Tulane University downstairs from the studio here where we are. I look at students with coveralls, overalls, or holes in the back of the butt, in their knees, just don't give a damn. But the people who were at this concert at that time had a collar and tie on, and a lot of people had expensive clothes. You see, even when you went to a football game at Xavier University, either at City Park, everybody put on collar and tie to watch a football game, even if the weather's warm. But today, everybody dressed a little different, you know.
But you're saying the thrust of this article is, it doesn't seem like, as I said, it sounds like it's very elitist, the person who wrote this.
Well, this is what I'm saying. Whoever it was.
Basically telling people, stop telling blacks, don't have collar.
Elgin Hodge, you wrote this there, as I think about it.

Well, you see, at that time, you're dealing with 1956, before integration was coming into its own, where the blacks who went to this particular program just wanted to get themselves into a system where they could say, well, we are as cultivated as whites at times, and then we can let our hair down at times, too, because we paid our money. And if I want to jump up in the aisle and dance, or if I wanted to be cool and sit down, or if I just wanted to hug somebody, if I just wanted to whistle at an entertainer, whatever, we could do that. That's what I think he's trying to say there.
